# Wayd — Complete Domain Context for LLMs

This document provides comprehensive context about Wayd's domain model, business rules, and architecture for AI agents and language models.

## System Overview

Wayd is an intelligent delivery management platform designed to give engineering leaders and teams end-to-end visibility into software delivery. It acts as a unified hub that synchronizes data from multiple business systems and combines it with capabilities those systems lack — connecting the dots so teams can see the full picture in one place.

Built with .NET 10, ASP.NET Core, Entity Framework Core, Next.js 16, React 19, and Ant Design. Follows Clean Architecture with Domain-Driven Design, organized as a modular monolith with a shared database.

### Ownership Model

Objects in Wayd have an ownership attribute:
- **Owned** — Created and managed within Wayd
- **Managed** — Synchronized from an external system (e.g., Azure DevOps) and read-only in Wayd
- **System** — Wayd system-owned, immutable by users

---

## Organization Domain

### Teams

Teams are the fundamental organizational unit. Properties:
- Name (up to 128 chars, unique across teams and teams of teams), Code (2-10 uppercase alphanumeric, unique), Description
- Active Date, Inactive Date (optional)
- Type: Team or TeamOfTeams
- Operating Model: Methodology (Scrum/Kanban) + Sizing Method (Story Points/Effort/Size/Count — which work item estimate the team's metrics read; no fallback between estimates, and the work process plays no part) + Time Zone (IANA id) + Commitment Grace Days + Working Week + optional Holiday Calendar (the whole-team reading; see Time Away and Holiday Calendars) + optional Cadence (Kanban only: `ReportingCadence`, 1-8 weeks plus an anchor date; reporting periods computed when read, no lifecycle)

Operating models have date ranges creating a history. New model auto-closes previous one (a move); editing a model in place is a correction of its whole period. A sprint takes its time zone and grace period from the model in effect on its planned start date (`GetTeamScheduleQuery`). Teams must always have at least one operating model; a new team gets Kanban and Count, with the time zone, grace period and working days from the Scheduling settings.

### Teams of Teams

Higher-level organizational unit containing child teams and other teams of teams. Provides rollup visibility across descendants. Same properties as Team but with child membership management.

A team of teams has its own effective-dated operating model (`TeamOfTeamsOperatingModel`) carrying only a Time Zone (IANA id), the zone its own rollups count days in; methodology and sizing stay with the child teams, which can mix them. It follows the same move-versus-correction rules as a team's model (both share the `OperatingModel` base) and always has at least one. The zone is never inherited: when a team or team of teams gets a new operating model, its zone is pre-filled from the parent team of teams' zone in effect on the new model's start date (membership is effective-dated too), falling back to the scheduling settings (`GetOperatingModelDefaultsQuery`).

### Team Memberships

Parent-child relationships with date ranges. States: Past, Active, Future.
Rules: One active parent per team, no overlapping date ranges, no circular references, both teams must be active.

### Allocations

How much of an employee's time a team or team of teams has over a date range, as a whole percent, optionally in a team member role. Behind the `team-capacity-management` feature flag. Owned per employee (`EmployeeCapacity`, whose id is the employee's, holding `EmployeeTeamAllocation` rows) because the rule spans teams: an employee's allocations never total more than 100% on any day.
Rules: membership is not required; one team can hold several allocations for a person in different roles; a change covers a date range and splits any allocation running past either end; allocations running on at the same percent are held as one; a move between teams or roles is one change. Changing a team's allocations needs `Permissions.Teams.Update` plus membership of the team or its team of teams, waived by `Permissions.Teams.Administer`. An inactive employee can be given time only with an end date, so a leaver's history can be filled in or corrected; time away can be recorded for them too. Deactivating an employee ends their allocations that day (`EmployeeDeactivatedEvent`, delivered durably); once their allocations have been changed since, a late or repeated delivery ends only those with no end. Deactivating a team or team of teams ends every employee's allocations to it on its inactive date and removes later ones (`TeamDeactivatedEvent`, delivered durably, so it follows the deactivation by a moment): each affected employee's `EmployeeCapacity` changes on its own and raises `EmployeeAllocationsChangedEvent` with the deactivation's actor and timestamp. Allocations to other teams are untouched, reactivating restores nothing, and a deactivation delivered after the team was activated again is skipped.
Capacity is derived, never stored: `GetTeamCapacityQuery` returns person-days per person over a date range, one person-day being one person allocated in full, and there, for one day of the team's working week (a team of teams uses the system defaults and this read counts only people allocated to it directly). Every person-day figure is net of the holidays of the calendar each person follows and their time away (see Time Away and Holiday Calendars); `WorkingDays` stays the team's own count, its working week less the holidays in its own calendar. A team member role with `CountsTowardDeliveryCapacity` off keeps its allocations out of delivery person-days while they still count toward the employee's 100%. The read also gives person-days per allocation and per role, each person's allocations to other teams, and what time away takes (`AwayPersonDays`, with each person's stretches as dates and percent, never the reason).
`GetTeamOfTeamsCapacityRollupQuery` (`GET teams-of-teams/{id}/capacity/rollup`) adds the teams beneath a team of teams, recursing through `TeamMembership` to any depth: a tree of nodes, each with the periods of the range it counts for, its own working days in them, the people allocated to it, its direct person-days and its totals including its children. A team counts only for the days its membership covers, intersected with the days its parent was itself in the hierarchy, so a child with several membership periods has several periods and a team that moved appears under each parent. An allocation counts once, on the team it was made to: a person allocated at two levels has time at each and is one person in the total. The rollup is read-only and stores nothing.
The Capacity section on team and team of teams pages is a view of these allocations over a date range and stores no plan: every edit goes through the allocation commands. On a team of teams it shows the direct allocations, editable, above a read-only tree of the teams beneath, and its totals and by-role lines cover both. `GetTeamAllocationProposalQuery` backs its Initialize action and saves nothing: one row per active member and role at what is left of their time from a start date, split evenly between their roles. A row stops the day before the member's next allocation to the team, and a member already on the team that day has none.
A capacity plan is the same view of a team's allocations over a fixed range, day by day: `GetTeamCapacityPlanQuery` (`GET teams/{id}/capacity/plan` and `GET teams-of-teams/{id}/capacity/plan`, up to 366 days) returns the team capacity read for the range plus, per person and role, the percent and person-days on each day of the team's working week, and per person the days a holiday, time away or time elsewhere decides (`TeamCapacityCalculator.DailyAllocation` and `DailyConditions`). Nothing is stored per day: a plan cell is a week counted from the plan's first day (all seven calendar days) or one day, and saving sends `ChangeEmployeeAllocationsCommand` with one change per edited cell, one command per person, so the days around the cell and every day outside the plan keep what they had. The sprint page's Capacity section is the plan for the sprint's planned dates; a member added there has an open-ended allocation and so is in the next sprint too, while a non-member's ends with the sprint.
`GetTeamsCapacityByPeriodQuery` (`Common.Application/Requests/Organization`) gives other modules the allocated, delivery and away person-days of many teams over many periods in a fixed number of reads, a team of teams counted as its rollup (`TeamPeriodCapacityCalculator`). Null when the flag is off (checked in the Organization handler).

### Time Away and Holiday Calendars

Behind the `team-capacity-management` feature flag, and held on the same `EmployeeCapacity` record as allocations. Three facts decide whether a person's allocated time is there on a day, kept apart: the team's working week (operating model), holidays (a `HolidayCalendar`) and time away (`EmployeeTimeAway` rows). A fourth, the person's working day, decides how much a day of their time is worth.
Holiday calendar: `EmployeeCapacity.HolidayCalendarId` is optional and points at a shared `HolidayCalendar` (the one for where the person works); many employees follow the same one. A person takes the holidays of the calendar they follow, otherwise the system default (`SchedulingSettings.DefaultHolidayCalendarId`), replacing rather than adding to it, and the same on every team. A team's operating-model calendar never decides a person's holidays; it only decides the whole-team reading (no allocations, or the flag off) and the team's own `WorkingDays` count. Set with `PUT employees/{id}/holiday-calendar` (`Permissions.Employees.Update`). A calendar an employee follows cannot be deleted. Holiday calendars are a separate thing from time away: a person's individual days off are always time away.
Working day: `EmployeeCapacity.WorkingDayHours` is optional (1-24, at most two decimal places; null = the system's `SchedulingSettings.WorkingDayHours`, default 8), the same on every team. Set with `PUT employees/{id}/working-day-hours` (`Permissions.Employees.Update`), raising `EmployeeWorkingDayHoursChangedEvent` with both ends. A person-day is one system working day, so a person's allocation and time away are shares of their own day and their time counts as `own / system` of a person-day (`WorkingDayLengths.DayShare`): a 4-hour part-timer at 100% is 0.5 person-days a day against 8. The 100% cap is still of their own time. Team days off are a share of everyone's day and are entered against the system's hours. DTOs that turn shares into hours carry the person's hours (`TeamCapacityPersonDto.WorkingDayHours`, `EmployeeTimeAwayDto.WorkingDayHours` with `OwnWorkingDayHours` and `SystemWorkingDayHours`); `TeamCapacityDto.WorkingDayHours` and `SprintDetailsDto.WorkingDayHours` stay the system's, the length of a person-day and of a team day off.
Time away: a date range (both ends required), `PercentAway` (1-100, the share of each day; the client enters it as Full day, Half day or hours of the person's working day, and reads it back the same way) and a `TimeAwayReason` (closed set: `PaidTimeOff`, `BusinessTravel`, `Training`, `Other`; lookup at `GET employees/time-away-reasons`). It is recorded per employee, never per team, never counts toward the 100% allocation limit, and lowers the person's time on every team in proportion to each allocation. Stretches may overlap but a day cannot total more than 100% away. Recording or changing needs an active employee; removing does not. "Away from one team only" is an allocation change, not time away.
Availability of a person to a team on a day = allocation percent x (day in the team's working week) x (not a holiday in the calendar they take) x (1 - share of the day away), in person-days times their working day as a share of the system's. `AvailabilityCalculator` (Organization.Application) is the one function every reader uses: `GetTeamCapacityQuery`, `GetTeamOfTeamsCapacityRollupQuery` and the sprint day weight; `TeamCapacityCalculator` applies `DayShare` to every person-day figure and to both sides of the day weight. `AvailabilityLoader` reads what it needs in three queries whatever the team size.
Who records time away: the employee, anyone above them in the manager chain at any depth (`ManagerChain.IsAbove`, which stops at a loop), or a holder of `Permissions.EmployeeTimeAway.Administer`. The first two need no permission claim; the commands require a linked employee. `TimeAwayAuthorization.CanManageTimeAway` answers for the commands and for `GET employees/{id}/time-away`, whose `canManage` flag and per-stretch `reason` it decides together: the reason is null for anyone else. The reason is in no domain event (`EmployeeTimeAwayRecordedEvent`, `EmployeeTimeAwayChangedEvent` with a `ReasonChanged` flag, `EmployeeTimeAwayRemovedEvent`, `EmployeeHolidayCalendarChangedEvent`, `EmployeeWorkingDayHoursChangedEvent`), so it never reaches the activity log, and it is in no team capacity DTO.
Sprint day weight: Work asks Organization through `GetTeamDayAvailabilityQuery` (`Common.Application/Requests/Organization`) for each day's allocated and available delivery time. The day's weight is available / allocated, counting only allocations in roles that count toward delivery capacity; Work then applies its own working week and the sprint's team days off (multiplying the weight by the share of the day the team works: 0 on a full day off, half on a half day). The query returns null when the flag is off (`IFeatureFlags`, checked in the Organization handler) or the team has no such allocation in the range, and has no entry for a day nobody is allocated on; in each case the day keeps the whole-team weight of 0 or 1 from the team's calendar and the sprint's days off.

### Deactivation Rules

The inactive date must be after the team's active date, and on or after the end of its latest parent membership; a latest membership with no end date blocks deactivation until it is given one. A team of teams applies the same rule to its latest child membership too (`Team.Deactivate`, `TeamOfTeams.Deactivate`).
Deactivating a team or team of teams ends allocations to it on the inactive date (see Allocations), whether or not `team-capacity-management` is on; the flag controls only the warning in the dialog. A past inactive date cuts allocations back to it, removing the time after it.

---

## Planning Domain

### Planning Intervals (PIs)

Fixed timeframe (typically 8-12 weeks) for coordinated delivery. Properties:
- Name, Description, Date Range, ObjectivesLocked flag
- Contains: Iterations, Objectives, Team associations, Sprint mappings

States based on current date: Future, Active, Completed.

Iterations are generated when the PI is created (`PlanningInterval.Create`), from an iteration length in weeks and an optional name prefix: back-to-back iterations from the PI's start named prefix + number, the last ending on the PI's end date however short and categorized Innovation and Planning (shown as **IP**). Afterwards they are edited, added and removed through Manage Dates (`ManageDates`).

PI detail page section rail: Overview, Plan Review, Objectives, Risks, Backlog, and Objectives Health under Reports. Sections are addressable as `?section=`. Team setup is in the Actions menu rather than a section — Manage Teams and Team Sprints (sprint-to-iteration mapping). The record facts panel carries dates, length, predictability, objectives-locked, description, and links.

#### PI Overview Page

Composed of four sections that adapt by PI state:

**At a Glance** — Summary card always shown:
- Timeline progress bar (elapsed vs. total PI duration)
- Teams count (delivery teams only, excludes Teams of Teams)
- PI Predictability % with completed/regular/stretch breakdown (Active/Completed only, hidden when no objectives)
- Avg Cycle Time across all team sprints (Active/Completed only, shown when data available)
- Three charts when objectives exist: Team Predictability (radar), Objectives By Status, Objectives By Health (open objectives — not Completed, Canceled or Missed — by health)

**Iterations** — Clickable cards per iteration, sorted by start date. Active iteration shows current day/total days and a health flag (On Track/At Risk/Off Track; see Iterations below). Cards are colour-coded: active = primary, Innovation and Planning = amber.

**Teams** — Grid of team performance cards (hidden for Future PIs). Each links to the team's Plan Review view and shows: Predictability with objective counts breakdown, Avg Cycle Time, Objective Status Chart, Objective Health Chart.

**Needs Attention — Objectives** — Active PIs only. Lists objectives with At Risk or Unhealthy health that are not yet completed. Sortable by health (Unhealthy first), progress, or team. Clicking an objective opens an inline details drawer.

### Iterations

Time-boxed periods within a PI. Properties:
- Name (unique within PI), Category (Development / Innovation and Planning, shown as IP), Date Range
- Dates must fall within PI range and not overlap
- Generated with the PI (see above), then managed through Manage Dates

Iteration health (active iterations only, client `calculateIterationHealth`): the work items still to finish in the mapped sprints against an even burn-down from the iteration's start to its end, as a share of the iteration's total — On Track at no more than 10 points behind (or ahead), At Risk above 10 up to 25, Off Track above 25. No flag while the iteration has no work items.

PI Iteration detail pages aggregate metrics from all mapped team sprints (cross-team view).

### Sprint Mapping

Each team's sprint maps to a PI iteration (one sprint per team per iteration, and at most one iteration per sprint across all PIs). Only sprints of type Sprint belonging to one of the PI's teams can be mapped; mapping a team's second sprint to an iteration replaces the first. Removing a team from PI removes its sprint mappings. The iteration's category decides a mapped sprint's sprint type unless the team set one (see Sprints).

PI Iteration metrics (`PlanningIntervalIterationMetricsResponse`): rolled up from the mapped sprints and from the PI's Kanban teams with no mapped sprint, which are measured over the iteration's dates (`GetKanbanTeamsWindowMetricsQuery`). Kanban teams add to Completed, In Progress, Unestimated and cycle time but not to Total or Not Started, which are scoped to sprints. Estimates are summed only when everything shares one sizing method. Cycle time is pooled (total cycle days ÷ item count, `CycleTimeSummary.Combine`), never an average of averages.

### Planning Interval Objectives

Team commitments within a PI. Properties:
- Team, Type (Team/TeamOfTeams, from the kind of team that owns it), Status (NotStarted/InProgress/Completed/Canceled/Missed)
- Start and Target dates (optional), Progress (0-100), Order, Closed date (stamped on moving to Completed/Canceled/Missed, cleared on moving back)
- IsStretch flag, Health Check (optional: Healthy/AtRisk/Unhealthy with expiration)
- Linked to work items that fulfill the objective

Business rules: Objectives can be created or deleted only while ObjectivesLocked is false. While locked, an objective's name and stretch flag are frozen (an update keeps the existing values); description, status, progress and dates stay editable.

Health checks (objectives and projects, `HealthReport`): the expiration must be in the future; recording a new check while the previous is current ends the previous at that moment, so at most one is current. After expiry the record has no health.

### Predictability

`PlanningInterval.CalculatePredictability`: (Completed objectives, stretch included / Committed non-stretch objectives) × 100, capped at 100. Stretch objectives stay out of the denominator, so completing one can make up for a missed committed one. Across the PI only Team objectives count (Team of Teams objectives are left out); per team, all that team's objectives count. Null for a Future PI or with no objectives; 0 when there are objectives but none committed.

### Risks

Potential circumstances that could impact delivery. Properties:
- Summary, Description, Team (set at creation, never changed), Reported By/On (the creator and the moment of creation), Status (Open/Closed)
- Category (ROAM): Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated
- Impact (Low/Medium/High), Likelihood (Low/Medium/High)
- Exposure: Impact + Likelihood, each Low=1/Medium=2/High=3 (Low <4, Medium =4, High >4)
- Assignee, Follow-Up Date, Response, Closed Date (set on close, cleared on reopen)

### Roadmaps

Visual timelines with hierarchical items. Properties:
- Name, Description, Date Range, Visibility (Public/Private), Managers (employees, min 1; the user creating or editing must be among them), State (Active/Archived — an archived roadmap rejects every change until activated again)
- Date ranges are inclusive; start and end may be the same day.
- Optional Color palette: named colors, one optional default, each value used once.

Item types:
- Activity: Date range, can contain children (other activities, milestones, timeboxes), ordered. Parent activities auto-expand to contain child dates; shrinking an activity behind its children is rejected; moving an activity without changing duration shifts the whole subtree.
- Milestone: Single date point. Created through the API only; the UI shows, opens and drags existing ones
- Timebox: Date range period

All items have optional Color. Roadmaps can be copied: a new Active roadmap with its own name, managers and visibility, keeping the description, dates and the full item hierarchy with item colors, but not the color palette.

### Planning Poker

Behind `planning-poker` feature flag. Real-time estimation via SignalR.

Estimation Scales: Named set of values (min 2). Configured in Settings.

Poker Sessions: Facilitator (the creator), uses one scale (locked after rounds begin), immediately Active on creation, then Completed. Rounds can be added, removed or relabelled and votes cast only while Active.

Rounds: Voting → Revealed → Accepted. Reset returns to Voting from Voting, Revealed or Accepted, clearing votes. Votes are submitted or withdrawn only during Voting.

### Story Maps

Behind `story-maps` feature flag. Real-time collaboration via SignalR. A user journey laid out as a grid, sliced into releases.

Structure: StoryMap (aggregate root) → Goals → Steps → Tasks. Swim Lanes and Personas are map-scoped and cut across that tree.
- Goal: the "backbone" — what the user is accomplishing. Ordered within the map. May have zero steps.
- Step: a stage within a goal, one board column each. Ordered within its goal. May have zero tasks. Movable between goals.
- Task: work under a step, positioned where its step column meets a swim lane row. `Order` is scoped per (step × swim lane) cell. Optional link to one work item (at most one task per work item per map; not an FK, not validated against the Work service).
- Swim Lane: horizontal slice (release/phase). Exactly one default lane per map, named "Tasks" at Order 0 — cannot be renamed, reordered, or removed, and always sorts first. Removing a lane reassigns its tasks to the default lane rather than deleting them, returning the moved count. Optional Start/End dates are descriptive only — unvalidated and unordered.
- Persona: audience tag (Name, optional Description, Color) scoped to one map. Set on goals, steps, and tasks by replacing the whole id list. Deleting a persona untags it everywhere, returning the untagged count. The board UI tags steps and tasks only; goals derive their filter state from descendants.
- Checklist Item: sub-item of a task (Name, IsChecked), persisted as JSON. Promoting one creates a task in the same step, always in the default swim lane. API-exposed; no board UI as of this writing.

Status: Active on creation; Archive is Active → Removed and one-way (no un-archive exists). Archived maps are read-only — every mutating method on the aggregate rejects with "This story map is archived and cannot be changed.", so the API enforces it rather than relying on the UI hiding the affordances. Delete is a separate soft delete and does not require archiving first.

Concurrency: the root carries a rowversion. The contended commands (goal/step/lane/persona reorders and step/task moves) run through `StoryMapMutation.Apply`, which reloads and re-applies once on `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` — concurrent drags on a shared board are an ordinary race, not an error to surface. The remaining commands are last-write-wins; they target a single field or node, so a race loses one edit rather than corrupting a sequence.

Notifications are best-effort: `StoryMapNotifier` logs and swallows hub failures, because handlers notify after committing and a broadcast error would otherwise make the client retry and duplicate the change. Reorder/move events carry the *applied* order read back from the aggregate, not the requested one, since the domain clamps and renumbers.

Ordering: zero-based throughout. Adds append at max(Order)+1; reorders renumber the collection contiguously. Task deletion does not renumber, so a cell's task order can go non-contiguous. Swim lane reorder pins the default lane at 0 and renumbers the rest from 1. `Step.Tasks` is returned unsorted — clients must sort by Order.

Permissions: all child mutations (goals, steps, tasks, lanes, personas, checklist, work-item links) require `Permissions.StoryMaps.Update` on the map. There are no per-entity permissions.

---

## Work Management Domain

### Sprints

Short time-boxed periods (typically 2 weeks) owned by teams. Properties:
- Name, Type (Sprint/Iteration), State (Future/Active/Completed, worked out when read from the actual or planned dates in the team's time zone), Date Range
- Team (optional), Ownership (Owned/Managed)
- Managed sprints have External Metadata (e.g., Azure DevOps iteration path)
- Actual Started/Completed instants, recorded by the team in Wayd and never synced. When absent the sprint follows its planned dates: start = beginning of the first planned day (never before the previous sprint ended), end = end of the last planned day (cut to the next sprint's start on overlapping AzDO dates), in the team's zone from the operating model in effect on the planned start. Together the Active period (`activeFrom`/`activeUntil`, end exclusive), which drives state, timeline, days remaining and health
- Commitment point (for metrics): Started, else the end of the commitment grace period after the planned start
- Start (after the previous sprint started, up to the planned end; first sprint from planned start − 3 days; only the team's next sprint), Complete (after its commitment point), Reopen (while no later sprint has started). One open sprint per team: starting the next completes the open one at the same instant, on confirmation; a filtered unique index backs it
- Lifecycle changes need Permissions.Iterations.Update plus membership of the team or its direct team of teams; Permissions.Iterations.Administer waives the membership. Unmapped sprints cannot be started or completed
- Events: SprintStartedEvent, SprintCompletedEvent, SprintReopenedEvent (carries the cleared Completed)
- Sprint type: Standard / NonStandard (`SprintType`), whether the sprint is comparable with the team's others; a NonStandard sprint is left out of the team's sprint metrics and listed there as excluded, and its own metrics still show. Worked out when read, never stored, in precedence order (`SprintTypeSource`): Team (the team's override, `Iteration.SprintTypeOverride`, set and cleared under the lifecycle permissions, events SprintTypeSetEvent / SprintTypeClearedEvent), PlanningInterval (the mapped PI iteration's category via `IterationCategory.ToSprintType()`: Development → Standard, InnovationAndPlanning → NonStandard), Default (Standard). Work reads the category through the cross-module `GetSprintIterationCategoriesQuery`; a mapping of a soft-deleted PI is ignored

### Team Sprint Metrics

A team's Velocity, Predictability and Say/Do across its most recent completed standard sprints (`TeamSprintMetrics`, `GetTeamSprintMetricsQuery`, `GET /api/organization/teams/{id}/sprint-metrics?sprintWindow=N`, MCP tool `Teams_GetSprintMetrics`). Worked out when read, never stored: each sprint's values come from its own scope report (`SprintScopeReport`), so they equal the sprint page's. Completed sprints (by timeline state, whether or not a completion was recorded) are assessed from the most recent back until the window is full, looking back at most three times the window. Left out and listed with a reason (`SprintMetricsExclusion`): NonStandard (dropped before its history is read), HistoryIncomplete, NoCommitment (nothing in the sprint at its commitment point). Each metric is summarized as the mean of the per-sprint values (not pooled totals), with min, max and population standard deviation, by item count and by estimate. The estimate is the team's sizing method now (its operating model in effect today, Count when it has none); a sprint measured in an earlier sizing method counts by item count only (`inEstimateAverages: false`), since estimates in different units are never averaged. The window defaults to the system setting `SprintMetricsSettings.SprintWindow` (default 7, 3–12), the same for every team; the team Overview and the sprint page's "Team avg" always use the setting (a NonStandard sprint shows no "Team avg"), the endpoint returns 404 for an id that is not a team's (a team of teams included), and the team's Sprint Metrics report opens at it and can be run over another window for that visit. Predictability is defined once, on `SprintScopeTotals` (completed ÷ committed, capped at 1), and returned on the sprint scope as `predictabilityCount` / `predictabilityEstimate`.

A Kanban team's cadence velocity (`TeamCadenceMetrics`, `GetTeamCadenceMetricsQuery`, `GET /api/organization/teams/{id}/cadence-metrics?periodWindow=N`, MCP tool `Teams_GetCadenceMetrics`). Worked out when read, never stored. Periods come from `CadencePeriod.Recent` over the operating models that have a `ReportingCadence` (read through `GetTeamScheduleHistoryQuery`): each model's periods follow its own cadence, in its own time zone, and are clipped to runs of consecutive models with the same cadence, zone and sizing method (`CadenceSchedulePeriod.ContinuesInto`), so a change to any of the three closes the open period the day before the new model starts and leaves earlier periods alone, while a model set for another reason does not. Across a zone change the older period ends exactly where the newer one begins. The Set operating model form fills in the current cadence. The current period and clipped (`isPartial`) periods are shown but not averaged. Velocity is Requirement-tier items with a Done-category status (Removed excluded) whose `DoneTimestamp` falls in the period, by count and by `WorkItemEstimate.Of` in the period's sizing method (`unestimatedCount` for items with none). Averages reuse `SprintMetricSummary` over ended, whole periods; `byEstimate` covers only periods in the team's sizing method now, and equals `byCount` under Count. The window is the number of ended periods, defaulting to `SprintMetricsSettings.SprintWindow` (3–12). No commitment, so no predictability or say/do. A team with no cadence returns no periods; a team of teams is a 404. The UI shows a Velocity report and an Overview card for a team whose current model has a cadence.

### Sprint Metrics

| Metric | Formula |
|--------|---------|
| Total | Number of items, and sum of their estimates in the sprint's sizing method |
| Completed | Items where status category is Done OR Removed |
| In Progress | Items where status category is Active |
| Not Started | Items where status category is Proposed |
| Remaining | Total − Completed |
| Completion Rate | (Completed / Total) × 100 |
| Velocity | Completed estimate (or completed item count) |
| Avg Cycle Time | Sum(Done − Activated) / Count for Done items with both timestamps |
| Unestimated | Count of items with no value (null) in the sprint's sizing method; 0 is an estimate |

"Completed" includes Done + Removed. Cycle time only calculated for Done items (not Removed) with both Activated and Done timestamps.

A sprint is measured in its team's sizing method on its planned start (`SprintSchedule.SizingMethod`, read through `WorkItemEstimate.Of`); a sprint with no team, or a day with no operating model, counts items. Responses carry counts always and `*Estimate` fields plus `SizingMethod`. A PI iteration rollup sums estimates only when every sprint shares one sizing method, otherwise its estimate fields and `SizingMethod` are null.

### Sprint Scope

What a sprint committed to and what became of it, worked out when read (never stored) from `WorkItemStateHistory` between the commitment point (effective start) and the effective end (`SprintScopeReport`, `GET /api/work/sprints/{idOrKey}/scope`). Only requirement-tier work types count; a type change out of the tier leaves scope, into it enters.

- Entry: **Committed** (in the sprint at the commitment point; taken out and put back stays committed) or **Added** (entered after it, before the effective end)
- Outcome, from the item's state when last in the sprint: **Completed** (Done), **Removed** (Removed-category, counts as completed), **CarriedOver** (unfinished and still in at the effective end, or moved to the team's next sprint on or after the last day), **Descoped** (unfinished and left before the last day, or on it for anywhere but the next sprint), **Remaining** (unfinished in a sprint not yet ended)
- Work already Done or Removed before `FinishedWorkCutoff` (the recorded start, else the start of the first planned day) is out of scope while it stays finished; reopened in the sprint, it is Added from then on
- Last day = the earlier of the last planned day and the day the sprint actually ended, in the team's zone
- Say/do = completed of committed ÷ committed, by count and by the estimate at the commitment point
- The sprint page shows Predictability = velocity ÷ committed, capped at 100% (finished added work counts), and Re-estimated = scope total at final estimates − committed − added. Each item carries `AddedAt` and `RemovedAt` (removed from the sprint, not a Removed status) and its original and final estimate
- Sprint metrics (`SprintWorkItemMetricsDto`) count requirement-tier work only, matching scope

### Sprint Burn

`SprintBurn` (`GET /api/work/sprints/{idOrKey}/burn`) reads scope and completed work, as counts and estimates, at the commitment point, at the end of each day in the team's zone, and at the effective end (or now). It reuses the scope report's per-item assessment (`SprintScopeReport.Assess`), so it agrees with the report at the start (scope = committed) and the end (completed = velocity; scope = total − descoped). An item is in scope from when it was committed or added while it is in the sprint; once it has left for good it stays if it left completed or carried over and drops if descoped; leaving and returning is a gap. Completed = in a Done/Removed category at the reading. Burn-down remaining = scope − completed; the ideal line runs from committed at the commitment point to zero at the effective end, falling in proportion to each day's working weight (`SprintWorkingDays.Weight`): 0 or 1 for a team read as a whole, and the share of its allocated delivery time that is there when Team Capacity Management is on and people are allocated (see Time Away and Holiday Calendars). Scope and burn load history through `SprintScopeHistoryLoader`.
`SprintCapacity` (`GET /api/work/sprints/{idOrKey}/capacity`, behind `team-capacity-management`) sets a sprint's delivery person-days over its planned dates beside its scope: before the commitment point the work in the sprint now (Planned), after it the committed work (Committed), by count under Count and otherwise in the sprint's sizing method. The expected scope is the velocity per person-day of delivery capacity over the completed sprints the team's sprint metrics count now that ended no later than this sprint, in the same unit and leaving out any with no capacity (so an older sprint draws on fewer prior sprints, or none), times this sprint's person-days (`SprintCapacityComparison`); `IsOverCapacity` is scope > expected on a sprint that has not ended. `Outcome` says why nothing was compared: NoCapacity, NoPriorSprints or NoPriorCapacity. Capacity comes from Organization through `GetTeamsCapacityByPeriodQuery`, so the endpoint returns 404 when the flag is off. Each period carries its sprint's team days off (`CapacityPeriod.DaysOff`, each a `TeamDayOff`: date plus `PercentOff` 1-100), which take that share of everyone's time on that team (never on teams beneath a team of teams), so capacity agrees with the ideal line; the sprint plan passes them too (`GET teams/{id}/capacity/plan?daysOff=yyyy-MM-dd[:percent]`), and the plan lists them in `teamDaysOff` with each day worth only the share worked. Team days off are stored in one column as `TeamDayOff` text (a bare date is a full day, so rows written before part days read as full days); `SprintTeamDaysOffChangedEvent` 1.1 adds `PartDaysOff`/`PreviousPartDaysOff`, where a listed date with no part-day entry is a full day. `SprintDetailsDto.Holidays` and `WorkingDays` let the Team Days Off form show days already off.
`PlanningIntervalCapacity` (`GET /api/planning/planning-intervals/{idOrKey}/capacity`, behind `team-capacity-management`) gives each team in a planning interval its allocated, delivery and away person-days for the whole planning interval and for each iteration, by the planning interval's own dates whatever a team's cadence. `GetPlanningIntervalCapacityQuery` (Planning) reads the interval's teams and iterations, sends `GetTeamDaysOffQuery` (Work: every team's sprint days off in a range, one read) and one `GetTeamsCapacityByPeriodQuery` with those days off per team (`TeamDaysOff`, applied wherever a team is counted, including beneath a team of teams). A team of teams is its rollup, so rows overlap and have no grand total; `hasAllocations` false is shown as a dash. A team's plan opens over the planning interval's dates.

Sprint health (`calculateCommitmentHealth`, client) measures velocity as a share of committed work against the share of time elapsed from the commitment point to the effective end — the ideal line's instants — with the usual thresholds (within 10 points On Track, 10–25 At Risk, more Off Track). Before a sprint has a commitment it falls back to completed vs. everything in the sprint over its days. The sprint page header, the Home active sprint card and the PI iteration page's team sprint cards all use it; those cards show Predictability, Velocity, In Progress (Carried Over once ended) and Say/Do from scope, and the Home card adds a compact burn-up. The PI iteration's own rollup still sums current items (#1002 tracks batching the cards' scope reads).
- A sprint is read up to now: before its commitment point it has no scope
- Deleted work items take their history with them, so they appear in no category
- `HistoryIncomplete` when any workspace holding the sprint's work (in history or currently) has no `Workspace.WorkItemHistoryBackfilledOn`, set the first time a history sync reads to the source's last batch

### Workspaces

Containers for work items. Properties:
- Key (2-20 uppercase alphanumeric, starting with a letter), Name, Description
- Work Process (defines available types/workflows), Ownership (Owned/Managed)
- IsActive (inactive prevents adding/removing items; a workspace is created and activated only with an active work process)

Managed workspaces: Synced from external systems, have external URL templates (the View Work Item URL, set in Wayd). Workspaces, work items, work processes and workflows come only from sync (`CreateExternal`); the API has no endpoint creating one. Work types and work statuses are synced too, though the API can also create them.

### Work Items

Fundamental unit of work. Properties:
- Key: {WorkspaceKey}-{Number} (e.g., PLAT-1234), the number being the item's id in the external system (its Azure DevOps work item id). Title, kept in step with the source on every sync. Tags.
- Type (WorkType), Status (WorkStatus), StatusCategory (Proposed/Active/Done/Removed)
- Priority, StackRank, Assignee, Team, Parent
- Estimates, kept separately: StoryPoints (sprint-level relative estimate), Effort (level of effort; Scrum's sprint estimate, and Agile features/epics), Size (CMMI). Each syncs from its own AzDO field; an item can carry several.
- Sprint/Iteration, Project (Portfolio tier only), ParentProject (inherited from parent)
- ActivatedTimestamp, DoneTimestamp, Created, LastModified. An item that went straight to Done/Removed takes its done timestamp as its activated one, and an activated timestamp later than the done one is moved back to it; DoneTimestamp is set only while the category is Done or Removed.

Supports: Parent/child hierarchy, dependencies, history, links, references.

Managed workspace items are read-only in Wayd, with one exception: a Portfolio tier item's project is set in Wayd (`UpdateWorkItemProjectCommand`, `Permissions.Projects.ManageProjectWorkItems`), and its descendants with no project of their own inherit it.

### Work Item Metrics (per item)

- Time to Start: Created → Activated (days)
- Cycle Time: Activated → Done (days). Formula: DoneTimestamp − ActivatedTimestamp
- Lead Time: Created → Done (days)

Portfolio tier items also show: a Progress chart (every descendant below the Portfolio tier, at any depth, by status category, Removed left out) and a Cumulative Flow chart (daily counts of the same items by category).

### Work Item Dependencies

Predecessor/successor relationships. Properties:
- Source (predecessor), Target (successor), Comment
- State: ToDo (source Proposed), InProgress (source Active), Done (source Done), Removed (source Removed), Deleted (link removed in the source)
- Health (`WorkItemDependency.CalculateHealth`), in order: Done → Healthy; Deleted → Unknown; Removed → Unhealthy; successor Active/Done/Removed while the predecessor is not done → Unhealthy; neither side planned → AtRisk; predecessor planned and successor not → Healthy; successor planned and predecessor not → Unhealthy; otherwise Healthy when the predecessor's planned date is on or before the successor's, else Unhealthy
- Scope: IntraTeam or CrossTeam (a read-side classification in `DependencyDto`)

An item's planned date is the last planned day of the sprint it is in; no sprint, or a date before today (UTC), counts as unplanned.

### Delivery Forecasting

Monte Carlo forecasts behind the `delivery-forecasting` feature flag. Read-only; view permission on the record is enough.
- Per-request options (not saved): history window (lookbackDays 14-365, default 90; UI offers 30/60/90/120/180), target date override, ignore dependencies (what-if), started work first (startedWorkFirst, default true: active backlog items ahead of proposed ones). Responses echo the options used.
- Throughput: Requirement-tier items reaching Done per UTC day over the history window ending yesterday, per team. Zero days count. Fewer than 10 completions → Not Enough History.
- Simulation: 10,000 trials resampling those days; confidence levels 50/70/85/95. Two-year horizon. Seeded by record id + date, so stable within a day.
- When (work item, PI objective, project): remaining work = open Requirement-tier items (Portfolio items expand to their open Requirement-tier descendants at any depth). Each item finishes when its team's run reaches its backlog position (active before proposed unless startedWorkFirst is false, then rank, then created). Open predecessors apply per trial through the whole chain; a cycle's closing dependency is ignored. Finish = latest item per trial. Objectives and projects also report the chance of finishing by the target date (objective target date or PI end; project planned end).
- How many (team): items finished by a target date, and the backlog item each confidence level reaches.
- Done and removed predecessors hold nothing up. Dependencies on a removed predecessor, and cycle-closing ones, are reported as ignored dependencies with a reason (Predecessor Removed, Closes a Cycle).
- Items that cannot be forecast (no team, not a backlog item, no history, blocked) are listed and excluded, making the forecast a lower bound. Unranked items sort after ranked ones, oldest first.
- Tier-based, never type-name-based.

### Work Item Hierarchy Rules

- Only Portfolio tier types can be parents
- A Portfolio tier child's parent must be a higher Portfolio level; Requirement and Task tier items can sit under any Portfolio level
- No self-links
- Portfolio tier items can be associated with PPM Projects; children inherit project, except Other tier items, which never take one

### Work Processes

Configuration linking work types to workflows. Properties:
- Name, Description, Ownership, IsActive
- Contains WorkProcessSchemes: WorkType ↔ Workflow mappings

Synced from the external system (an Azure DevOps process) with its work types and workflows; in Wayd a process is only activated or deactivated. Rules: each type once, only active processes assignable to workspaces, cannot be deactivated while an active workspace uses it.

### Work Types

Categories of work items. Properties: Name (immutable), Description, Level, IsActive. The tier comes from the level; editing a type changes only its description and level.

Tiers:
- Portfolio: Container types, multiple hierarchy levels (Epic, Feature)
- Requirement: Base-level team work (User Story, Bug)
- Task: Child types (Task, Sub-task)
- Other: Non-standard, not in backlog views. Synced work types start here until placed on a level

### Work Type Levels

Default system levels: Epics (Portfolio L1), Features (Portfolio L2), Stories (Requirement L1), Tasks (Task L1), Other (Other L1). Only the Portfolio tier takes custom levels, added at the bottom and reordered; level names are unique.

### Workflows

Status progression definitions. Properties: Name, Description, Ownership, IsActive.
Contains WorkflowSchemes: WorkStatus + WorkStatusCategory + Order.

Created only by sync (`Workflow.CreateExternal`): each Azure DevOps work item type's states become a workflow, each state's category mapped to a work status category. Rule: each status appears once per workflow. A status's category is set per workflow (on the WorkflowScheme), so one status can sit in different categories in different workflows. No minimum count, category coverage or ordering rule exists. Not to be confused with a Status Workflow (below), the engine behind Product Management statuses.

### Work Statuses

Individual status values (e.g., "New", "In Progress", "Done"). Name is immutable; no category of its own. Reusable across workflows.

### Work Status Categories

Fixed normalization set:
1. Proposed — Not yet started
2. Active — Currently being performed
3. Done — Completed
4. Removed — Removed without completion

Enables cross-workflow metrics (cycle time, throughput, completion rates).

### Work Item History

Effective-dated state imported from the source's revisions: one period per stretch of time during which the tracked fields (iteration, status, work type, team, assignee, Story Points, Effort, Size) didn't change. "What was true at time T" is a range filter (`ValidFrom <= T AND (ValidTo IS NULL OR ValidTo > T)`). Source values (status and type names, the source's iteration id) are kept beside the resolved ones. History is deleted with its work item. Every revision read is also kept as a source revision, and periods are built from them: a revision that arrives out of order (an item that moved between projects) rebuilds the item's periods, and revisions an item is missing are fetched from the item itself. A full sync replays the source's revisions onto it without deleting anything; revisions already stored are skipped.

---

## Project Portfolio Management Domain

Permissions: two independent checks, both required for any mutation. (1) The permission claim `Permissions.{Projects|Programs|ProjectPortfolios|StrategicInitiatives}.{View|Create|Update|Delete|Import}` gates reaching the endpoint. (2) Delivery leadership gates which records may be changed: the actor must hold Owner or Manager on the record itself or on any ancestor — project ← program ← portfolio, inheriting downward. Sponsors and project Members are deliberately excluded. `Permissions.ProjectPortfolioManagement.Administer` is a domain-wide grant that substitutes for leadership everywhere in PPM but never for the permission claim; it is the only way to seed the first Owner on a new portfolio, since a portfolio has no ancestor. Leadership gates status transitions, detail and timeline edits, role assignment, project key/program/lifecycle changes, health checks, scores, and ranking. It does NOT gate viewing, creation (Create permission), deletion (Delete permission), or bulk import (Import permission — imported records have no leadership at the moment they are created). Every managed action requires a linked employee record.

### Portfolios

Top-level container. Properties:
- Name, Description, Status, Date Range, Roles
- Optional ScoringModelId: active scoring model assigned to enable project priority scoring
- Owns project ranking: every project in the portfolio has a required fractional Rank sort key; the displayed Position is derived at read time per portfolio

Status lifecycle: Proposed → Active → Closed (from Active or OnHold; all programs and projects completed or canceled) → Archived (read-only). Activate sets today as the start date and Close today as the end date (the import can backdate both). OnHold ↔ Active exists in the domain (`Pause`/`Resume`) but no endpoint calls it: a portfolio reaches OnHold only through the portfolios import. Programs, projects and strategic initiatives can be created only in an Active or OnHold portfolio. Only Proposed portfolios can be deleted.

Roles: Sponsor, Owner, Manager. Owner/Manager confers delivery leadership over the portfolio and everything beneath it; Sponsor does not.

Contains: Programs, Projects, Strategic Initiatives.

Portfolio scoring rules: only Active scoring models can be assigned. Clearing or changing the assignment disables/changes future scoring only; existing project score snapshots remain intact.

Portfolio ranking rules: projects are ranked from creation and new projects are placed at the bottom. Portfolio Owners/Managers (or a PPM administrator) can reorder Proposed, Approved, and Active projects from the portfolio Ranking section; ranking uses the same leadership rule as every other portfolio management action. Ranking is human-managed and independent of computed priority score. Dragging is disabled while the board is sorted, filtered, or searched because drops must be expressed against the natural rank order. Completed/Canceled projects are hidden from the ranking board but keep ranks. Ranks use fractional values for cheap inserts; the PortfolioRankRebalance Hangfire maintenance job re-spaces dense ranks to clean whole-number gaps.

### Programs

Groups related projects. Properties:
- Name, Description, Status (Proposed/Active/Completed/Canceled), Date Range, Roles (Sponsor/Owner/Manager)
- Strategic Theme Tags

Lifecycle: Proposed → Active (requires start and end dates) → Completed or Canceled; Proposed → Canceled directly. Rules: Only active programs accept projects. Completing, or canceling an active program, needs every project completed or canceled. Active and Completed programs must keep a date range. Projects cannot be removed from a completed or canceled program. Only Proposed programs with no projects are deletable.

### Projects

Most feature-rich entity. Properties:
- Key (ProjectKey, 2-20 uppercase alphanumeric), Name, Description, BusinessCase, ExpectedBenefits
- Status, Date Range, Expenditure Category, Lifecycle, Roles (Sponsor/Owner/Manager/Member)
- Strategic Theme Tags
- CurrentScore summary: latest project priority score value, scorer, timestamp, and scoring model name
- Rank: required fractional sort key within the portfolio; Position is the derived 1-based display rank in project lists

Status lifecycle: Proposed → Approved (requires lifecycle) → Active (requires start and end dates) → Completed/Canceled. Approval is optional: `Project.Activate` accepts a Proposed project with dates, though the UI offers Activate on a Proposed project only once it also has a lifecycle. Cancel works from any open status. Only an active lifecycle can be assigned, and a closed project's lifecycle cannot be assigned or changed. Every transition requires delivery leadership (see the domain Permissions note above).

Projects can also move backwards, which programs and portfolios cannot. Legal reverts: Completed/Canceled → Proposed, Approved, or Active; Active → Proposed or Approved; Approved → Proposed. Entry requirements apply whichever direction a status is reached from, so returning to Approved still needs a lifecycle and returning to Active still needs dates — a project cancelled straight from Proposed may therefore only return to Proposed. A revert additionally requires a written reason, recorded in the status history, and is rejected while the parent program or portfolio is closed.

Status history is append-only, ordered by a per-project monotonic Sequence rather than by timestamp (imports write several transitions at one instant). A revert appends a row rather than editing the one it supersedes, so a project can enter the same status more than once.

Key can be changed (cascades to all task keys), as can the assigned program and lifecycle — all three require delivery leadership. Deletable only while the project has never left Proposed — reverting to Proposed does not restore deletability, because deleting would destroy the status history. At most one program.

Project priority scoring: if the parent portfolio has an assigned scoring model, project Owner/Manager, portfolio Owner/Manager, or program Owner/Manager can record scores. Each score is an immutable ProjectScore snapshot with per-project Sequence ordering, frozen criterion ratings, calculated outputs, scorer, timestamp, and model id/key/name. Re-scoring creates a new history entry and updates CurrentScore.

### Scoring Models

Reusable formula-driven models for consistent ranking. Properties:
- Name, Description, State (Proposed/Active/Archived)
- Criteria: rated inputs with unique tokens, optional descriptions, optional weights, optional rating scales
- Rating scales: named ordered levels, each with label and decimal value
- Outputs: ordered arithmetic formulas over criterion tokens and earlier output tokens; exactly one output is primary

Lifecycle: Proposed is editable/deletable; Active is locked and assignable; Archived is retired. Activation requires at least one criterion and one valid primary output. Formulas support arithmetic over decimals and reject unknown tokens, malformed expressions, function calls, and divide-by-zero evaluations.

### Project Lifecycles

Templates of stages. States: Proposed (editable) → Active (locked) → Archived.
Must have min 1 stage to activate. Only Proposed deletable/editable.

### Project Stages

Concrete instances created from the lifecycle's stages. Properties:
- Name (from template, not editable), Description (editable), Status (NotStarted/InProgress/Completed/Canceled)
- Date Range, Progress (0-100%), Roles (Assignee)
Rules: Date range is optional unless root tasks have dates, in which case it automatically rolls up to cover the child range span. A stage range cannot be manually shrunk behind its children's dates, nor can its dates be cleared while root tasks have dates.

### Project Tasks

Hierarchical work items within stages (WBS). Properties:
- Key: {ProjectKey}-{Number}. Name, Description, Type (Task/Milestone)
- Status (NotStarted/InProgress/Completed/Canceled), Priority (Low/Medium/High/Critical)
- Progress (0-100 for tasks, 0 or 100 for milestones), Order, Dates, Effort (hours)
- Dependencies (Finish-to-Start, soft-deleted), Roles (Assignee)

Rules: Milestones cannot have children or be InProgress. Cannot delete tasks with children or active dependencies. No circular moves (a task cannot move under itself or a descendant).

Task dependencies are recorded, not enforced: a successor's status and dates can change whatever its predecessor's state. Both tasks must be in the same project, a task cannot depend on itself, and a pair has at most one active dependency; chains are not checked for cycles. They are managed through the API and MCP only — the Plan section neither shows nor edits them. `GetCriticalPathQuery` is a stub that returns an empty list. Parent task date ranges automatically roll up from child dates (minimum start through maximum end). A parent task cannot be manually shrunk behind its children's dates, nor can its dates be cleared while children have dates. Shifting a parent task shifts its dated descendants.

### Strategic Initiatives

High-level strategic efforts within portfolios. Properties:
- Name, Description, Status (Proposed/Approved/Active/OnHold/Completed/Canceled)
- Date Range, Roles (Sponsor/Owner), KPIs, Projects. No strategic themes.

Lifecycle: Proposed → Approved → Active → Completed; Canceled from any open status. OnHold is defined, and Complete accepts it, but no method moves an initiative into or out of it and the import rejects it. Rules: Only created in Active/OnHold portfolios. Deletable in Proposed/Approved. Completed/Canceled = closed: no KPI or linked-project changes.

### KPIs

Measurable indicators on strategic initiatives. Properties:
- Name, Description, StartingValue, TargetValue, ActualValue (from latest measurement)
- Prefix, Suffix, Direction (Increase/Decrease)
- Checkpoints: planned target values at specific dates with at-risk thresholds
- Measurements: actual recorded values over time, with the employee who recorded them

Checkpoint and measurement dates must be unique per KPI. A measurement date cannot be in the future. A starting value must be below the target for Increase and above it for Decrease.

### Expenditure Categories

Project cost classification. Properties:
- Name, Description, State (Proposed/Active/Archived)
- IsCapitalizable, RequiresDepreciation, AccountingCode
- Settings frozen after activation (historical accuracy)

---

## Strategic Management Domain

### Visions

Organizational direction. Properties:
- Description, State (Proposed/Active/Archived), Dates (start/end instants, stamped by the transitions)

Rules: Only a Proposed vision can be activated, which stamps now as its start; only an Active one archived, which stamps now as its end. Only ONE Active vision at any time. Archived visions cannot overlap in dates, and a vision cannot be activated inside the most recently archived vision's range (`VisionAggregate`). Archived = immutable.

### Strategies

Approach for achieving vision. Properties:
- Name, Description, Status (Draft/Active/Completed/Archived), Date Range (optional start, optional end)
- Independent of visions.

Status is set directly on create and update; no transition order or dates are enforced.

Visions and strategies have no UI: they are managed through the API only. Strategic themes have screens.

### Strategic Themes

High-level organizational priorities. Properties:
- Name, Description, State (Proposed/Active/Archived)

Rules: Proposed → Active → Archived, one step at a time (the import sets any state directly). Only Proposed deletable. State changes publish domain events (PPM maintains synchronized copy).

Cross-domain usage: Tags on Projects and Programs for alignment tracking (creating a project or program, or importing one, accepts only active themes; the update commands do not check state). Strategic initiatives carry no themes. A project's effective themes are its own when it has any, otherwise its program's.

---

## Demand Management Domain

Asks for delivery capacity before anyone has decided to do them: upstream of PPM and Work, and never required by either. Behind the `demand-management` feature flag; API only until #1043 adds screens. Its context (`IDemandManagementDbContext`) does not extend `IWaydDbContext` and the module references no other module (`DemandManagementBoundaryTests`).

### Intake Requests

One ask, shown as a Request. Properties:
- Number (`Key`, sequential across the install, so moving desks never renumbers), Title, Description, Expected Benefits (optional prose: what gets better, and for whom; named for `Project.ExpectedBenefits`)
- Requester and Submitter (employees; they differ when submitted on someone's behalf), Desk (exactly one, chosen by the requester), Channel
- Need-By (optional): a `LocalDate` that never travels without its `NeedByBasis` and a reference; a Commitment also records who made it and on what date. Date, basis and reference change together in one event, and clearing the date clears all of them
- Origin (optional, fixed at creation): source system, external id, URL; unique on source system + external id
- Assigned Reviewer (optional ownership, never an approver; must review on the desk), Participants

Rules: every request is Proposed until the review workflow (#1045). Edit lock by status category — Proposed: the requester or an Update holder; Active: Update holders; Done and Removed: nobody. Editing also needs the substance tier, because the update carries the description. Delete is refused once a request has outcomes or status history beyond its first status (neither exists yet). No product and no strategic themes on a request in v1.

### Read Tiers

Each field and each event belongs to one tier (`IntakeRequestReadTier`), and the DTOs are built per tier rather than filtered afterwards:
- **Summary** — number, title, desk, status, requester, channel, assigned reviewer, tags, need-by date with basis and reference. `IntakeRequestSummaryDto`; what lists return
- **Substance** — description, expected benefits, submitter, participants, origin, evidence, replies, score. `IntakeRequestSubstanceDto`, null when withheld
- **Internal** — internal notes and triage reasoning; Review on the desk only

Who reads what (`IntakeRequestReader`, expressions that run in SQL): on an Open desk everyone with View reads summary and substance; on SummaryOnly everyone reads the summary and the substance goes to the request's own people (requester, submitter, participants) and to anyone who reviews on any desk; on Private only the desk's reviewers and the request's own people know the request exists — it is absent from lists, counts and history for everyone else, and a direct read answers 404. A private desk withholds even the summary from reviewers of other desks. History is filtered by event tier in the query (`IActivityLogReader.ReadEventTypes`), so pages and totals cover only what the reader may see; a reader without the substance also gets every entry without its actor (employee, client and the payload's `actor`), because the submitter is substance. Request numbers are install-wide, so a gap discloses that hidden requests exist (accepted).

The details DTO answers what the reader may do — `canEdit`, `canReview` and `canAddParticipants` — by the same rules the commands apply; a client shows actions from these flags and never re-derives them. The list takes `mine=true` for requests the caller requested or submitted, filtered on the server because the submitter is substance and not in the summary. `GET /api/demand-management/employee-options` lists active employees by name for anyone with View on intake requests, since most requesters cannot list employees through Organization. The need-by basis families are a lookup too (`GET intake-requests/need-by-basis-families`, code and name), so a client groups and labels bases without hard-coding "Fixed for us" and "We chose it".

### Intake Desks

A review responsibility, not a team or department. Properties: Name (unique), requester-facing Description, Visibility (`Open`/`SummaryOnly`/`Private`), Is Requester Selectable, Is Open, Requester May Add Participants (private desks), Reviewers (an explicit employee list, never derived from teams). Nothing is seeded; an administrator creates desks (`POST intake-desks`, Administer). Changing desks and re-routing requests arrive with #1118.

Review = `Permissions.IntakeRequests.Review` + being named a reviewer on the request's desk, waived by `Administer` (which never replaces the permission). Reviewers assign the owning reviewer and remove participants. Participants are added by a desk reviewer, or by the requester or submitter except on a private desk that does not allow it.

### Intake Channels

Where a request came from; a company-defined vocabulary referenced by id with an active/archived state. Eight are seeded once (business stakeholder, customer feedback, support, sales and account management, innovation program, regulatory and compliance, security, engineering). Administering channels arrives with #1120.

---

## Status Workflow Engine

Cross-cutting. Any module whose records carry a status registers an owner type and resolves through `IStatusResolver`; the engine holds no module's vocabulary.

### Status Workflows

Properties: Name, Description, OwnerType, State (Draft/Published/Archived), IsSystem, Key, Statuses (ordered).

Rules: Statuses are added, removed or reclassified only in Draft — records carry a denormalized category and alias, so moving one on a live workflow leaves every record disagreeing with the status it points at. Renaming, re-describing and reordering statuses are allowed until the workflow is archived. System workflows cannot be modified, published by a user, or archived. Publish requires every alias the owner type declares required. Archive requires the workflow to be unassigned. Clone copies the statuses into a new Draft and is the only route by which a published or seeded workflow is changed.

### Workflow Statuses

Properties: Name, Description, Category (Proposed/Active/Done/Removed), Alias (int, 0 = none), Order.

Rules: Names and aliases are unique within a workflow. The category is the rollup; the alias is the well-known meaning platform logic reads instead of the name. ReclassifyStatus changes both, Draft only.

### Workflow Transitions

Transition Mode is AnyToAny (default) or Restricted, set in Draft only. Under Restricted, only the workflow's WorkflowTransitions (from → to, each with optional Transition Conditions: `RequiresReason`, and `RequiresPassedApproval`, reserved and not attachable until an evaluator exists) are allowed; `SetTransitions` replaces the whole set. A Restricted workflow publishes only for an owner type whose descriptor declares `SupportsRestrictedTransitions`, and must allow every required Workflow Move the owner type declares. Aggregates enforce it through `StatusRef.AllowedFrom` and `ConditionsFrom` in `StatusTrackedEntity.ApplyStatus`, without loading the workflow; a record's initial status and `SwitchWorkflow` are exempt. See the Domain Glossary for the full rules.

### Workflow Assignments

Which workflow a scope's records use. Properties: OwnerType, ScopeId (null = organization-wide, the only scope in use), WorkflowId.

Rules: ReassignTo requires a published workflow of the same owner type and a complete remap whose endpoints match.

### Status Remap

A transient mapping between two workflows. AutoMap resolves by alias, then exact name, then category when the target has exactly one candidate; anything left is Unresolved. Never persisted — the confirming command rebuilds it and layers operator decisions on top, which is safe because AutoMap is pure over two loaded workflows.

### Reassignment

Migrates every record of an owner type onto the target workflow. Records move first, the assignment flips last, so an interrupted run leaves the assignment pointing at the workflow the records are still on and re-running is correct. Crosses the module boundary through IStatusRecordMigrator, implemented in Infrastructure because Common cannot see a Product.

### Status Transitions

Every status change, with from/to, actor, timestamp and sequence. Written by BaseDbContext draining the aggregate during SaveChanges. OwnerType + RecordId identifies the record; RecordId is deliberately not a foreign key, so nothing cascades to it: every Product Management delete removes the record's transitions itself in the same save (StatusHistoryRemoval.Stage).

---

## Following

A follow (`Follow`, in `Wayd.Common`, table `Notifications.Follows`) is one employee's choice to keep one record in their Following list: owner type, owner id, employee, followed instant, keyed on all three of the first so following twice is a no-op. Behind the `following` feature flag. In-app notifications (#1126) will use follows; until then following notifies nobody.

Owner types are registered strings, as for status workflows: each module declares a `FollowOwnerDescriptor` (`ppm.project`, `ppm.program`, `planning.planning-interval-objective`) and an `IRecordReadRule` that says which records the caller may read (with an unhealthy flag and a closed flag per record, for filtering in SQL) and what each looks like now (key, name, status, lifecycle category, health, progress, the people who lead it — a project's or program's owners and managers, an objective's team — and dates). Adding a followable record is a registration, not a schema change.

The Following list is paged in SQL across every owner type at once (`UNION ALL`), sorted by last change (default) or by follow date, newest first by default or oldest first (`direction`), where "last changed" is the newest activity-log entry the record's own Activity section lists — its own entries under its aggregate type, and entries naming it as related — and a record with none counts as the least recently changed. The activity log is read by id and aggregate type together, since records in different modules can share an id. It narrows by owner type, by a "needs a look" view — `Unhealthy` (current health check unhealthy), `ChangedRecently` (activity in the last seven days), `Closed` (lifecycle Completed or Canceled; a missed objective counts as Completed) — and by a search on name or exact key. Counts per type and per view come from the same query, after readability.

**Following grants nothing.** A record can be followed only by someone who can read it through its own read rule, and a follower who loses access sees it leave their list and its count; a follow is never an input to authorization. It is also not participation: a participant is given a record and access with it, a follower chose one they could already see. Follow and unfollow are idempotent and act only for the caller — there is no adding a follower. API: `/api/me/follows` (`Me_Follow`, `Me_Unfollow`, `Me_GetFollowStatus`, `Me_GetFollows`, `Me_GetFollowCounts`, `Me_GetFollowedRecord`).

---

## Product Management Domain

Gated by the `product-management` feature flag (disabled on first deploy). Authorization is permission-claim only — unlike PPM, no membership or leadership requirement on a record.

### Products

The catalog of what the organization builds. Properties:
- Name, Description, Type, Parent, Status, Tags, External Id, Key

Rules: Nests by containment; a node with no parent is a root. A product cannot become its own ancestor — the domain refuses a move into its own subtree, and the UI picker omits that subtree. Durable across the Projects that change it.

Facets are changed through separate commands, each enforcing its own rule: UpdateProductDetails (name/description), RetypeProduct, ReparentProduct, ChangeProductStatus, TagProduct/UntagProduct, LinkProductExternally.

### Product Types

What the organization calls a kind of node. A table, not an enum, so phase-two additions (capability flags, distribution model, sourcing, allowed-parent rules) stay additive with no backfill. Properties:
- Name, Description, IsReleasable, IsActive, Order, Key

Seeded: Product Line, Platform, Module, Interface (not releasable); Product, Application, Service, Tool, Library (releasable).

Rules: IsReleasable decides whether VERSIONS can be cut against a node. A product cannot be retyped onto a non-releasable type once versions exist. It does NOT gate Releases (announcements), which may sit under any node. The seeded types are system types: they cannot be renamed, have their releasability changed or be deleted, only deactivated. Another type can be deleted only while no product carries it (`DeleteProductTypeCommand`); one in use is deactivated instead, because existing products still resolve their type. Product types have no screen: they are managed through the API (and MCP) with `Permissions.ProductTypes.*`.

### Product Tags

Classification along an axis, grouped into categories (Platform, Tech Stack, Compliance). Only Platform (allows many: web, ios, android, desktop, cli, server) is seeded, as a read-only system category; the rest are added by the organization. Properties:
- Category (Name, Description, AllowsMany), Tag (Name, Description, IsActive)

Rules: Grouped rather than flat so "what platform is this?" is a query rather than prior knowledge. Carries what does *not* change behaviour; the type system carries what does. An inactive tag a product already carries stays offered, so a save cannot silently remove it. A tag no product carries can be deleted (DELETE /product-tag-categories/{id}/tags/{tagId}, ProductTagCategories.Delete); one in use is deactivated instead, and tags on a system category can be neither.

### Product Dependencies

One product needing another over a period — Storefront Web depending on Identity Service since March. Properties:
- Product (the one that has the dependency), DependsOnProduct, Strength (Hard or Soft), InteractionStyle (optional set: Synchronous, Asynchronous or both — a `[Flags]` enum in the domain, a list of names at every boundary; null means not recorded, never "neither"), Description, Period (a FlexibleDateRange of days; the end day is included and null while it still holds)

Rules: Owned by the product that has the dependency; the product depended on only reads them. Any product can depend on any other except itself and anything above or below it in the tree, which is composition. Cycles between unrelated products are allowed. Record the most specific product known (the service, not its platform); parent views roll links up when read and nothing rolled up is stored — a link from a child to an outside product appears under the parent's Depends On, and a link with both ends inside a product's subtree appears in neither list.

Strength is required with no default: Hard means the product stops working without the other, Soft that it degrades but keeps working. A later downtime view counts a provider's downtime against a consumer only through a Hard link, so defaulting either way would skew it.

History: a dependency that stopped is ENDED (kept, still counts for the period it held); one recorded by mistake is REMOVED (deleted, reason required). Terms (strength and recorded interaction styles) never change on a link — Change Terms (`ChangeDependencyTerms`) from day D ends the link on D-1 and opens a new one from D carrying the description, raising Ended then Added; so terms cannot change on the day the link started, nor on an ended link, nor in the future. The exception is recording styles on a link that had none, with the strength unchanged: that fills them in place as a details update, since nothing about the dependency changed. A null style leaves recorded ones alone. Dated by day rather than instant because dependencies are entered by hand; periods include their end day, so a link may start and end on the same day and a later link on the same pair starts the day after the earlier one ended. The description can be edited on any link, ended ones included (`UpdateDependencyDetails`, which refuses to change styles already recorded). A pair of products has at most one open link, and links on the same pair cannot overlap. Dates cannot be in the future. A product is refused deletion while any link, open or ended, names it on either end. A move is refused when it would put two products with an OPEN link between them above and below each other — checked across the moved subtree and the new parent's lineage, in both directions; an ended link does not block it.

Imported with POST /api/product-management/products/dependencies/import (Import Products permission; columns ImportId, ProductId, DependsOnProductId, Strength Hard|Soft required, InteractionStyles optional (Synchronous;Asynchronous), Description, StartsOn default today, EndsOn): PerGroup by ProductId, so a product's rows apply together or not at all while other products are kept; a product's rows are applied in date order, a strength change is two rows on the pair, and a rerun is refused by the overlap rule rather than duplicated. 50,000-row cap. Events (ProductDependencyAdded/Ended/DetailsUpdated/Removed) are raised on the dependent product and name the product depended on as a related aggregate, so both products' Activity lists them.
UI: the Dependencies section is a grid; the product's Overview also draws a one-hop map (React Flow) of open links only — used-by on the left, depends-on on the right. A link rolled up from a descendant is drawn from that descendant, never as an edge from the parent. Every product nests inside boxes for what contains it, on both sides and to any depth, from the ProductDependencyDto's ProductPath/DependsOnProductPath (full chains from each end's root); containment is never drawn as an edge. Nodes are keyed per column, so a product with links on both sides is drawn once in each. Nodes and boxes link to their product; the canvas has zoom, fit, fullscreen and save-as-image (PNG/SVG, rendered from the graph rather than screenshotted). An All / Hard only control on the canvas redraws the map from hard links alone (map only; the grid is not filtered): products and boxes left with no link are not drawn, the per-side cap applies after the filter and the overflow count is of hard links, and a product with only soft links keeps its card with an empty state. The choice is kept for the browser session (sessionStorage), and a saved image is not marked as filtered. A capped column ends in a "+N more" node that draws the rest in place; the card's corner link is always "View all". Any product off to one side can be expanded (+ on its outer edge) to draw its own links one column further out, outward only (a provider's providers, a consumer's consumers), with no depth limit. An expansion uses the per-product GET dependencies endpoint (no dedicated API) but keeps only links the expanded product holds itself — the endpoint's subtree rollup is discarded — and drops links touching the subject's subtree. A product is drawn once per side, in the column where it was first found; a link reaching it again is drawn as a backward edge (left side to right side) or a same-column curve, and each link is drawn once. Each expansion is capped with its own "+N more for X". Collapsing removes everything the expansion reached, nested expansions included. Expansions are kept per subject in sessionStorage. Renaming or moving a product invalidates every dependency list, because rows carry both ends' names and ancestry.

### External Id
