A product's identifier in the system that owns it — repository, pipeline, registry package. Set through LinkProductExternallyCommand, never as part of a details edit, so a rename cannot clear it. Null clears the link. Nothing consumes it yet; it exists so a later automated feed can be matched against hand-curated products.

### Versions

A versioned cut of one releasable product node — the ARTIFACT half of delivery (Wayd API 4.12.0). Owner key `delivery.version`. Properties:
- Number (free text version string), Name, TargetDate (LocalDate — a plan), CutAt (Instant — the build or tag that froze scope), ReleasedAt (Instant — when production received it), Sequence, Notes (engineering), Status, Product

What happened is an Instant and what is planned is a calendar date. The UI enters and shows CutAt/ReleasedAt as date and time in the viewer's own time zone (Cut and Mark Released default to now). Versions whose cut/released values predate instants carry 12:00 UTC on their original date — the same calendar day in every zone from UTC−11 to UTC+11 — and can be fixed with CorrectDates.

NOTE ON NAMING: the domain property is `Number`, not `Version` — C# forbids a member matching its type's name. It is still a version string and is never parsed as a number.

Rules: Describes what was cut, never where it went — rollout lives on Deployment. A version with no deployment is a complete record, which makes version-first hand-entry workable. States: Planned → Ready → Released, or Withdrawn.

Version numbers are never parsed or compared — versions are not sorted by number. Lists put unreleased first, then released newest-first.

Each lifecycle move is one-way and sets a moment and a status together: Cut (raising VersionCutEventV2) refuses a version already cut, MarkReleased (VersionReleasedEventV2) refuses one already released, and a withdrawn version refuses being released (though a released one can be withdrawn). Cutting is NOT a prerequisite for releasing — a version may be marked released with no CutAt, which is what makes historical import possible. Where both exist, ReleasedAt cannot precede CutAt, compared as moments to the minute.

Because those moves refuse to run twice, a separate correction action exists: CorrectDates fixes a TargetDate, CutAt or ReleasedAt recorded wrongly and leaves the status alone, writing no StatusTransition and raising VersionDatesCorrectedEventV2 (carrying both ends of each change) to the audit trail instead. Without it, fixing a released moment would mean withdrawing and re-releasing, appending two status transitions that never happened to an append-only history. All three values are sent together, so an omitted one is CLEARED rather than left unchanged. A value may be ADDED as well as changed — cutting is not a prerequisite for releasing, so a cut moment discovered later is a correction, not a lifecycle step. TargetDate and CutAt may be cleared; ReleasedAt may not (the status would contradict it), and the whole action is refused on a withdrawn version. The one ordering rule that remains: ReleasedAt cannot precede CutAt.

RevertRelease is the separate action for a version marked released IN ERROR — it never shipped and the record was wrong. It moves the version back to Ready (or to the workflow's initial status where it was never cut), clears ReleasedAt, requires a reason, and raises VersionRevertedEventV2. It is NOT a withdrawal: withdrawing asserts a real shipment was pulled and is terminal, so recording a mistake that way leaves an append-only history claiming a withdrawal nobody performed. Refused when the version has no ReleasedAt, and on a withdrawn version. Mirrors the RevertStatus pattern on PPM's Project.

The V1 event types (VersionCutEvent, VersionReleasedEvent, VersionRevertedEvent, VersionDatesCorrectedEvent), which carried dates, are frozen and obsolete — kept only so payloads already recorded still deserialize; only the V2 types, which carry Instants, are raised.

### Releases

What was ANNOUNCED TO CUSTOMERS — the product half of delivery (Wayd 2026.07). Owner key `delivery.release`. Properties:
- Version (its own free-text label, e.g. "2026.07"), Name, Target Date, Released Date, Sequence, Notes (product), Status, ProductId (NULLABLE), Versions, Packages

DO NOT CONFUSE WITH Version. A release answers "what did we tell customers?"; a version answers "what version of this one artifact?". One release commonly spans several versions, and a version may ship without ever being announced. The release's own `Version` label (2026.07) is distinct from the version numbers it carries (4.12.0).

Rules: A release is NEVER CUT — cutting freezes an artifact's scope and belongs to Version; a release's scope is whichever versions and packages it carries. It therefore has NO CutDate, and its CorrectDates takes only target and released dates.

ProductId is OPTIONAL and typically names a product LINE rather than a leaf: a release spanning product lines has no single owner. It is deliberately NOT gated on ProductType.IsReleasable — that gate asks whether an artifact can be cut against a node, which is Version's question; a product line is usually not releasable and is exactly what an announcement sits under. GetReleases(productId) EXCLUDES releases with no product, because a release belonging to no single product would be misstated by listing it under one.

CONTENTS arrive by two routes and a release may use both: ReleasePackages (the usual route — the package is the deployment unit) and Versions carried DIRECTLY (a single artifact that shipped on its own, rather than inventing a package of one). Both routes are set TOGETHER by a single SetReleaseContents (PUT {id}/contents), which is a WHOLE-SET REPLACEMENT of both: an omitted id is removed, and both lists empty clears the release. They are one operation because the double-count rule below spans them — split in two, each half would judge that rule against a release only half-changed. Contents are frozen once the release is announced or withdrawn.

THE DOUBLE-COUNT RULE: a version reachable through one of the release's packages CANNOT also be carried directly. Otherwise one release announces the same shipment twice. The rule is applied to what the release ends up containing, NOT to what it contained before — so moving a version out of the direct list and into a package that ships it is allowed in one call, being one change of mind rather than a double count. The handler resolves the covered versions from the packages IN THE REQUEST and passes them to the aggregate, which cannot load a manifest itself. A manifest line with no VersionId (a component carried forward from before Wayd held it) covers nothing and never conflicts.

An EMPTY RELEASE IS LEGITIMATE and is not a draft — a repackaging or a pricing change is announced with nothing deployed. Unlike a package, which must be assembled from at least one component.

MarkReleased is REFUSED while any version or package the release carries has not shipped — this is the one claim a release can make that its own contents contradict, and it is the only real invariant a release has. Withdraw says NOTHING about the versions carried: an artifact that shipped has shipped whatever the market was later told, so each version is withdrawn separately. RevertRelease works as it does on a version, and requires a reason.

### Release Packages

Several component versions shipped as one coordinated unit. Properties:
- Version, Name, Status, Components (manifest of component versions)

Rules: Where a package exists it owns the deployment and its component versions do not — one pipeline run shipping fifteen services counts once, not fifteen. NOT a SAFe Release Train (that is TeamOfTeams in Organization).

Each manifest entry carries a Kind: Changed (the component changed in this package) or CarriedForward (it shipped unchanged). Recording the carried-forward lines is what makes the manifest a full statement of what was in the box. A component may appear only once per manifest. An entry's VersionId is optional and there is deliberately no foreign key behind it — a carried-forward line often names a version that was never cut in Wayd — so the version string is stored as text in its own right.

SetManifest is a WHOLE-MANIFEST REPLACE, not a delta: components carry no id and are not individually addressable, so the call must send every line the package should end up with, and an omitted line is removed. It is refused once ReleasedAt is set or the status category is Removed, and refuses an empty manifest.

CorrectDates (PUT {id}/dates) fixes a package's target date or released moment recorded wrongly and leaves the status and its history alone, raising PackageDatesCorrectedEventV2 with both ends of each change. Because a set ReleasedAt is what closes the manifest and makes MarkReleased refuse, the correction can CHANGE the released moment of a released package but can neither CLEAR it nor ADD one to a package not yet released — MarkReleased records the first. Refused on a withdrawn package. A package's ReleasedAt is an Instant — the completion of the pipeline run that shipped it, written as the CI/CD timestamp with its offset and never converted — while its TargetDate is a LocalDate plan. Packages released before ReleasedAt existed were migrated to 12:00 UTC on their original date.

A Version has NO PackageId. Membership is recorded only by the package's manifest, and is queried the other way with GetReleasePackages(containingVersionId) for one version, or containingProductId for every package carrying any version of a product — there is no ?packageId= filter on versions, and no VersionDto.Package. A package likewise carries no owning release: it may serve more than one, so membership lives in the ReleasePackageInclusions join.

### Deployments

One version or package reaching one environment. Properties:
- Version OR Package (exactly one), Environment, Environment Category, Artifact Id, StartedAt, EndedAt, Status

Rules: The substrate every delivery metric is computed from. States: In Progress → Succeeded, Failed, or Rolled Back.

VersionId XOR PackageId is validated in three places and answered with a 422 — supplying both or neither is refused. StartDeployment also refuses an inactive environment.

EnvironmentCategory is FROZEN on the deployment as it stood when the deployment ran; it is never resolved through the environment on read. A deployment's category can therefore legitimately differ from its environment's category today. Reclassifying an environment changes what FUTURE deployments count as and rewrites nothing.

A deployment is never edited. Once started it is only ever completed: Succeed/Fail while IsComplete is false, and RollBack only from Succeeded (a failed deployment never reached its environment, so there is nothing to revert). A completion cannot predate the start; a rollback cannot predate the completion. A PRODUCTION success also records the release of what shipped, through the ordinary MarkReleased: an unreleased version it carried, or for a package the package and each CHANGED component version (carried-forward ones shipped earlier), becomes Released at the deployment's completion — imported rows that succeeded or were rolled back included, since a rollback shipped first. A released moment already set is never replaced (a filled one is indistinguishable from an entered one), withdrawn records are skipped, and a record cut after the completion is left for the aggregate to refuse.

### Deployment Environments

Named deploy targets, globally scoped and ordered into rings for progressive rollout. Properties:
- Name, Category (Development/Testing/Staging/Production/Other), Ring Order

Rules: Named DeploymentEnvironment because Environment would shadow System.Environment. Category is a fixed enum, not a workflow — a classification rather than a state. Every production-scoped measure counts on the category, not the free-text name. Reclassifying raises its own event because it changes what is counted from then on; past deployments keep the category they froze.

Environments are RETIRED (PUT /{id}/active) as the everyday way out — historical deployments point at them. DeploymentCount exists so a caller can show what retiring or deleting would affect. Update and reclassify are both refused on an inactive environment.

Withdrawing and retiring are the everyday way out and are all Update. DELETE is its own grant — Delivery.Delete (versions, packages, deployments), Releases.Delete, DeploymentEnvironments.Delete — for a record made by mistake or to purge a retired product's history. Every delete removes the record's status history in the same save and raises a *DeletedEvent (Deployment/Environment/Package/Release/VersionDeletedEvent); the activity log and audit trail are always kept. A delete never edits another aggregate — it refuses instead:
- Deployment: any state.
- Environment: takes every deployment into it; when it has any, also needs Delivery.Delete (a delete that takes records of another resource needs that resource's Delete, checked only when there are any).
- Release package: takes its manifest and every deployment of it; refused while any release lists it.
- Release: any state, announced included; takes its contents list, keeps the versions and packages it listed. Deleting an announced release (whose contents are frozen) is how a package it lists becomes deletable.
- Version: takes every deployment of it; refused while a release lists it or a package manifest names it (manifest lines hold VersionId without a foreign key).
- Product: unchanged refusals (children, versions, manifest, either end of a dependency), so a retired product is purged bottom up: releases → packages → versions → dependencies → product.

### Delivery Overview

Version activity over a window, for one product subtree or the whole catalog. GET product-management/delivery-overview (from, to, productId, timeZone) and /recent. `timeZone` is an optional IANA zone (default UTC; the web app sends the browser's) — the window and the per-day activity buckets are that zone's days, so a late-evening release counts on the day it happened locally. The MCP tool DeliveryOverview_GetDeliveryOverview takes the same parameter.

Measures: versions released per week, and mean cut-to-released latency — the real elapsed time between CutAt and ReleasedAt, in fractional days, not a count of calendar days. Both count VERSIONS ONLY — a release package is a bundle of versions, and counting one would count the same shipment twice.

Rules: scoping to a product covers that node AND every descendant, so a non-releasable grouping rolls up its children rather than reporting nothing. Cut-to-released excludes versions released without ever being cut — they carry no latency, and counting them as zero would make the average improve as history is backfilled; the measured and released counts are both returned. A previous-window figure is null rather than zero when nothing shipped then, since a rise from zero is not a trend. Activity is the catalog subtree flattened depth-first with a Depth per row, so the view indents rather than groups — grouping listed a node that is both releasable and a parent twice. A grouping carries no days at all. The recent feed reads status transitions, not the records' own CutAt/ReleasedAt — a record's moment says the state it is in now, while a transition says when it changed; it includes release packages, and drops them when scoped to a product.

### Rollout

What is running in each environment. GET product-management/deployment-environments/rollout (includeInactive).

Rules: an entry is the latest deployment that SUCCEEDED AND STAYED SUCCEEDED, not the latest deployment — a rollback replaces its own deployment's status, so admitting only Succeeded leaves the version before it as the answer, and a failed attempt does the same. Every entry is keyed on the PRODUCT: a package deployment is expanded into its manifest and each component competes for its own product's slot. Keying on the package instead reports every bundle ever deployed as running, because successive bundles carry the same components and no bundle supersedes a differently-numbered one. Derived, never stored. Retired environments are excluded by default.

### Delivery Metrics

Computed over a window from production deployments:
- Deployment Frequency — completed production deployments. Rolled-back deployments count (they reached production); in-flight and failed do not.
- Change Failure Rate — share of completed production deployments that failed or were rolled back. Production only: a failure caught in staging was prevented.

Reported as explicitly unavailable, with reasons, rather than approximated:
- Lead Time for Changes — needs a link from a deployment back to the change it carried (commit or work item).
- Time to Restore Service — needs an incident record. A rollback is not a substitute.

Counts and totals accompany every average so windows and scopes combine without average-of-averages bias.

---

## Integration Domain

### Azure DevOps Boards Connector

One-way sync (Azure DevOps → Wayd; synced records are Managed):
- Azure DevOps Process → Wayd Work Process (initialized per process)
- Azure DevOps Project → Wayd Workspace (initialized per project, once its process is)
- Azure DevOps Work Item → Wayd Work Item
- Azure DevOps Work Item Type → Wayd Work Type (new types land in the Other tier); its states → Work Statuses and a Workflow
- Azure DevOps Team → Wayd Team, through the workspace's Team Mappings; a work item's team is the team that owns its iteration
- Azure DevOps Iteration → Wayd Sprint: type Sprint when it has no child iterations and both dates, otherwise type Iteration. Mapping a sprint to a PI iteration is done in Wayd
- Azure DevOps revisions → Work Item History
- Azure DevOps identity → Employee, via ExternalIdentityMapping

Requires a PAT with Work Items (read) and Project and Team (read); Wayd never writes back. Each org linked by one connection. Background sync via Hangfire (differential and full).

People on a work item (Assigned To / Created By / Changed By) resolve through `ExternalIdentityMapping`, keyed on the external system's stable identity id rather than an email address. Resolution is three-tier: an admin's mapping or ignore decision wins and is never revised by a sync; otherwise the reported address is auto-matched against every work email an employee has; otherwise the identity is recorded as Unmapped for review on the connection's People tab. Mapping or ignoring an identity repoints work items already synced, using the identity ids stored on WorkItemsExtended — so an item synced before those ids existed needs a full sync before a mapping can reach it.

### People Connectors

Entra (Microsoft Entra ID through Microsoft Graph) and Workday (the Staffing SOAP service) sync employees and contingent workers into the Organization domain's Employee records, with their work email addresses. At most one People connection can be active at a time, so one person never becomes two employees. Connectors declare capabilities (`ConnectorCapability`: WorkItems, People, AiProvider); the capability, not the connector, decides which sync runs. Azure OpenAI is an AI provider and syncs nothing.

### MCP Server

The API exposed as agent tools over the Model Context Protocol, two ways: the hosted endpoint `/mcp` on the API (Streamable HTTP, behind the `mcp-server` feature flag, 404 while it is off; sign-in or a Personal Access Token in `x-api-key`), and the `@wayd/mcp` npm package (a PAT, Node.js 22+). Both offer the same tools under the same names; the hosted endpoint also serves the product skills in `skills/` as prompts and through a skills tool. Tools act as the signed-in user, so permissions and delivery leadership apply as in the UI.

---

## Architecture Patterns

### CQRS with Wolverine
All operations are commands (writes) or queries (reads) dispatched through `IDispatcher` (backed by Wolverine). Controllers are thin. Handlers must be public. Handler dependencies are constructor-inlined by codegen (service location is NotAllowed); a dependency with an internal implementation class needs an AlwaysUseServiceLocationFor<T>() allow-list entry in WolverineConfiguration — codegen write fails naming the type otherwise.

### Identity vs Principal
`ICurrentUser` is pure identity (who is the caller: id, name, email, employee link). Authorization questions go through `ICurrentPrincipal` (HasPermission/HasAnyPermission), which derives the caller's permission set from `ICurrentUser` + `IUserService` and caches it per scope. Don't add permission or claim APIs to `ICurrentUser`. `ICurrentUser.Kind` classifies the caller: User (authenticated or impersonating background scope), Anonymous (unauthenticated HTTP — denied all permissions), or System (no HTTP request, no acting user: jobs, durable messages, startup — granted all permissions, audited as the well-known SystemIdentity.UserId). Only real user ids are propagated across job/message boundaries; absence resolves to System (the rule lives in CurrentUser.Kind only). Assumption: background work never originates from anonymous callers — anonymous-enqueued work would run as System, so propagate an explicit anonymous marker if that is ever needed.

### Background Jobs
Recurring and on-demand work (syncs, cross-domain replication, maintenance) runs as Hangfire jobs behind `IJobService`, whose DTOs carry no Hangfire types. Managed at Settings → Background Jobs: job lists by state (Processing/Scheduled/Enqueued/Failed/Succeeded/Deleted), per-job detail with arguments, state history and failure stack trace, recurring schedules, and worker servers. Permissions: `BackgroundJobs.View` to read, `.Run` to trigger/requeue/schedule, `.Delete` to delete jobs or remove schedules.

Job counts come in two incompatible kinds and must not be presented as one set: current counts (Enqueued/Scheduled/Processing/Failed, plus retained Succeeded/Deleted via SucceededListCount/DeletedListCount) agree with the matching job list, while all-time Succeeded/Deleted are running counter totals that keep climbing after job records are purged.

Not every job type can be scheduled. `SchedulableBackgroundJobTypes` is the single source of truth: it gates the recurring endpoint and supplies `BackgroundJobTypeDto.IsSchedulable`, which the UI filters its picker on. The cross-domain replication syncs (Projects, Teams, Iterations, Strategic Themes) are run-on-demand only. Scheduled jobs execute as System — a cron trigger has no HttpContext, so `WaydJobFilter` stamps no UserId and `CurrentUser.Kind` resolves to System; `EnqueueSystem` exists to undo that stamping on the manual path, which does have one.

### Bulk Imports
Every area with CSV import exposes one `POST .../import` endpoint per file kind (multipart, field `file`; strategic initiatives, release packages and releases take a second file whose lines nest under a row of the first). A post records the file as an ImportProcess (a "run"), queues it to a background worker, waits up to `Imports:ResponseWaitSeconds` (default 5) and answers with the run — 200 if finished, else 202 with a Location. Rows reference each other by `ImportId`, the caller's own per-file key (≤128 chars, case-insensitively unique, defaults to row position); it is never written onto created records — each applied row reports the id of the record it created, and the next file references those ids.

Constraints: an ImportDefinition declares `Atomicity` (PerRow: rejected rows are reported and the rest kept; Atomic: one transaction, one bad row keeps all of it out; PerGroup: rows sharing a group key the definition derives from the row, or from the whole file where one row cannot say — stored as ImportProcessRow.GroupKey at submission — apply together or not at all, the rest kept. A PerGroup chunk never splits a group; when a row is rejected the runner detaches everything the attempt tracked and reruns the chunk without the rejected groups, marking their other rows "Not applied: another row for the same {noun} was rejected (import id X)". The registry refuses a PerGroup definition with more than one pass, since each pass saves before the next. Every PPM import is PerGroup: portfolios, programs, projects and strategic initiatives group by the record the row creates — a row is not per-row-safe because it creates and then transitions, so a rejection partway must discard what it staged, which only the PerGroup path does — while tasks and stages group by the project, because a child task names its parent's ImportId in the same file, the per-project task number advances as rows apply, and a project's stages are read against one another. The PPM finalization import, the last step, closes programs and portfolios once their contents are in (things can be added only to an open program or portfolio, but one closes only when everything inside is closed): PerGroup keyed on the record it closes, applied as a whole set with programs before portfolios. The planning interval, objective, risk, team, team membership, team member and strategic theme imports are Atomic. The Product Management imports are PerGroup too, except deployments, which are PerRow (no natural key, and a row is added only after its whole walk succeeds): products group by the root of their tree, derived from the whole file because a child names its parent's ImportId in the same file; versions and dependencies by ProductId; packages, releases and environments by the record the row creates, a package's manifest and a release's contents riding on its row), `MaxRows` (50,000 PerRow — employees — and PerGroup product dependencies; 10,000 Atomic, and every PPM and other Product Management import, which applies PerGroup or PerRow but keeps the lower cap until a larger file is proven end to end), `PreflightMaxRows` (defaults to MaxRows; set to 10,000 by the employee import, because a preflight is one transaction rolled back at the end and cannot release locks chunk by chunk, so the file size is the lock time) and `ChunkSize` (500; PerRow and chunked PerGroup imports save and record progress per chunk, a stop takes effect at a chunk boundary). Over-cap and empty files are rejected before queuing. An optional `submissionGroupId` query parameter (any non-empty GUID) is recorded on the run so files posted as one operation can be found together; it is a label only and links nothing — a program still names its portfolio by the id the portfolio run reported. A run is claimed at most 3 times before it ends Failed; `import-stall-recovery` (every 5 min) republishes a run queued 15 min without a worker and fails one silent for 30 min; `import-retention-sweep` (nightly) clears stored row payloads 30 days after completion, after which rows cannot be retried. Both jobs are scheduled on first start. Runs are visible under Settings → Imports; seeing a run requires the permission that submits its kind, or the read-only View Imports oversight grant.

### System Settings
Organization-wide settings are typed sections in code, stored one JSON row per section in `App.SystemSettings`. A section is a record implementing `ISettingsSection<TSelf>` with a stable `Key`, whose property initializers are its defaults; a missing row or property reads as the default, so adding a setting needs no migration. Modules read a section through `ISettings<TSection>` (cached, 5-minute expiry across API instances) and never touch keys or JSON. Saves go through `ISystemSettingsStore.Save`, which validates with the section's FluentValidation validator, guards concurrent saves with a row version, and raises `SystemSettingsSectionValuesChangedEvent` carrying every value before and after, so each change is in the Activity log. Section keys and property names cannot be renamed once shipped. The first section is Scheduling (Settings → System → Scheduling, key `scheduling`): `DefaultTimeZone` (IANA id, default UTC), `DefaultCommitmentGraceDays` (0–14, default 1) and `DefaultWorkingDays` (default Monday–Friday), which pre-fill new team operating models and are never inherited when reading a team's own values; `DefaultHolidayCalendarId`, the holidays of anyone and any team with no calendar of their own; and `WorkingDayHours` (default 8), the length of a person-day. The Sprint Metrics section (Settings → System → Sprint Metrics, key `sprintMetrics`) holds `SprintWindow` (3–12, default 7): how many of a team's most recent completed standard sprints its velocity, predictability and say/do are averaged over, the same for every team. Permissions: `SystemSettings.View` and `.Update`.

### Result Pattern
Handlers return Result<T> from CSharpFunctionalExtensions. No exceptions for business logic.

### No Repository Pattern
EF Core DbContext used directly in handlers.

### Vertical Slices
Each service: Domain (entities, value objects) → Application (commands, queries, DTOs, validators) → shared Infrastructure.

### Feature Folders
Application layer organized by aggregate root: {Feature}/Commands/, {Feature}/Queries/, {Feature}/Dtos/.

### Time Handling
NodaTime types (Instant, LocalDate). Never DateTime.UtcNow — always inject IDateTimeProvider.

### Frontend Patterns
- NSwag-generated typed client for API calls (never authenticatedFetch directly)
- Ant Design theme tokens (never hardcode colors)
- Redux Toolkit + RTK Query for state/data
- CSS Modules with antd CSS variables preferred over theme.useToken()

---

## Key Relationships Summary

```
Organization
  Team → participates in → Planning Interval
  Team → owns → Sprint
  Team → commits → Objective
  Team → tracks → Risk
  Team → assigned to → Work Item

Planning
  Planning Interval → contains → Iteration
  Sprint → mapped to → Iteration (1 per team per iteration)
  Objective → linked to → Work Item
  Predictability = completed objectives (stretch included) / committed objectives, capped at 100%

Work Management
  Workspace → uses → Work Process → defines → Work Type ↔ Workflow
  Workspace → contains → Work Item
  Sprint → contains → Work Item
  Work Item → has → Status → placed in → Status Category (by its type's workflow)
  Work Item → depends on → Work Item (predecessor/successor with health)
  Work Item → parent of → Work Item (parent Portfolio tier; a Portfolio child needs a higher-level parent)

PPM
  Portfolio → contains → Program → groups → Project
  Portfolio → contains → Strategic Initiative → tracks → KPI
  Strategic Initiative → links → Project
  Employee → holds roles on → Portfolio, Program, Project, Strategic Initiative
  Project → has → Lifecycle → defines → Stage → copied to → Stage → contains → Task
  Strategic Theme → tags → Project, Program

Strategic Management
  Vision (one Active); Strategy (independent of visions)
  Strategic Theme → referenced by → PPM entities

Product Management
  Product → contains → Product (tree); Product → depends on → Product (not within its own tree)
  Version → cut against → releasable Product
  Release Package → manifest of → Versions
  Release → carries → Versions and Release Packages
  Deployment → of one → Version or Release Package → into → Deployment Environment
```
